claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–base metal HEA nanoparticles on TiO2 is governed by support-assisted hydrogen spillover.
Enhanced catalytic performance is governed by the same support-induced spillover mechanism that enables HEA formation.
Noble metals such as Ru or Rh on TiO2 generate highly reducing spillover hydrogen species.
Spillover hydrogen migrates from noble-metal sites to base metals and rapidly reduces base metals such as Ni or Cu at low temperature.
Spillover hydrogen simultaneously reduces both noble-metal and base-metal precursors.
Synchronized precursor reduction promotes atomic intermixing and formation of chemically homogeneous HEA nanoparticles.
TiO2-assisted spillover can enable alloys of normally immiscible noble and base metals.
The TiO2 spillover strategy can be applied to synthesize TiO2-supported HEA nanoparticles.
Synchronized reduction lowers kinetic barriers for atomic diffusion and mixing.
Complete alloying enhances catalytic activity through synergistic effects among alloy components.
TiO2-supported CoNiCuRuPd HEA nanoparticles exhibit high activity and outstanding stability during CO2 hydrogenation.
The spillover mechanism should operate effectively at 150–300 °C and ambient pressure under hydrogen.
Relative to SiO2, TiO2-supported synthesis should produce a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to SiO2, TiO2-supported synthesis should reduce phase segregation.
Relative to SiO2, TiO2-supported synthesis should yield higher catalytic performance.
SiO2 is a minimally spillover-active support expected to cause sequential or incomplete reduction and poorer alloy formation.
The effective temperature window, hydrogen partial pressure, and reduction kinetics may vary with the particular metal combination.
Particle size and precursor dispersion can influence spillover efficiency.
An otherwise matched TiO2-versus-SiO2 comparison at 200 °C under hydrogen can test the proposed mechanism using elemental mapping, phase analysis, and catalytic measurements.
